Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old male whose trauma type is rape, the trigger 'Military Topics' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and memory items coherently suggest interpersonal/close-contact danger (touch, strangers, shouting, doors, vivid sensory reliving), but military-related talk implies a trauma context that is otherwise absent. This is not supported by the threat or memory content and does not fit the formulation as a plausible trigger tightly linked to the presented threat-memory pattern.

vignette: Six months ago, Marcus was waiting in the service corridor of a downtown office complex to deliver finalized client ledgers to a senior partner. The corridor was narrow, lit by flickering fluorescent panels, and he was entirely alone. When the heavy fire door at the end of the hall slammed shut, the concussive echo made him turn, and before he could step back, a man emerged from the stairwell and raised his voice. The shouting that followed vibrated in Marcus’s ribs, sharp and unmodulated. The first contact was a sudden, forceful grab at his shoulder that made him jolt forward, his nervous system overriding any attempt to process the situation. What happened next left a sensory imprint that would outlast the event itself: the sharp, chemical bite of the man’s peppermint gum, the stark angle of a ceiling tile, and the complete, suffocating realization that he was trapped in a space with no clear exit. By the third week, Marcus’s routine had begun to fracture. At eighteen, he was already working as a tax consultant in his family’s practice, a role that required him to consult with clients across different floors and occasionally in unfamiliar satellite offices. He quickly found that he could no longer enter conference rooms without mapping every door and window first. The unfamiliarity of new client spaces made his chest tighten; he simply could not assess the threat in rooms where he didn’t know the sightlines or how the locks functioned. He began declining assignments that took him outside the firm’s main wing, sticking to the original floor where every corridor and doorway felt familiar. When senior staff knocked or swung glass doors open, the sudden auditory spike made him drop his clipboard, his breath catching in the same rhythm it had in that service hallway. The memories did not arrive as narratives. They surfaced as sudden, high-contrast photographs: the scuff mark on a linoleum floor, the specific tilt of a man’s jacket, the way light caught a metal handle. During a quarterly review in a quiet consultation room, a wave of pure alarm hit him without any accompanying picture. He was suddenly certain he was in danger, his hands trembling around his pen, until the astringent taste of peppermint coated his tongue. The taste always returned first, a physical anchor dragging the terror forward, proving that the past was still physically present in his mouth. He came to believe that any room where he couldn’t see the door could suddenly shift from neutral to threatening, and he stopped scheduling lunch meetings in unfamiliar cafes or client offices where he couldn’t control who entered or how loud the conversations might become. His alertness settled into a constant baseline. When a client reached over to hand him a document, Marcus flinched, his shoulders shooting up before his brain could register the gesture. He was certain that strangers walking toward him in the firm’s lobby or in elevators carried a latent threat, forcing him to angle his body away and keep his posture rigid. Being alone with other men became an exercise in calculation; he arranged client meetings only when a colleague sat in the hallway, and he kept his own office door propped open during every consultation. His avoidance patterns and his threat monitoring operated in parallel, each demanding his attention as the months passed. The occupational toll was immediate: client files sat unprocessed in his drawer, and his father noticed the defensive posture Marcus adopted during phone calls, the way he measured his words as if bracing for a sudden escalation. Now, Marcus sits across from me, his knuckles pale around his notebook, finally ready to step into a treatment room. He is not looking for someone to tell him to ignore his alarms or push through the discomfort. He is hoping for a way to separate the past from his daily environment, to sit in an unfamiliar conference room without his pulse spiking, to work alongside male clients without his body preparing for a repeat of that corridor. What frightens him most is the quiet certainty that he will spend the rest of his life bracing for a door to slam, tasting copper in an empty room, and flinching at the sound of a raised voice that belongs entirely to the present.
